text: FOR JSON turns an entire query result into a JSON string, right inside T-SQL. AUTO is the simplest version: add it to the end of a query, and you get back one JSON array with one object per row, using your column names as the keys.

Bring a join into the picture, and AUTO infers the nesting on its own. Based on the order the tables appear in your FROM and JOIN clauses, the second table's columns get nested as a sub-object automatically -- no extra instruction needed.

PATH takes the opposite approach: explicit control. A dotted alias like Product dot Name becomes a nested JSON object with Product as the outer key and Name inside it. You decide the shape directly through your aliases, instead of relying on how the join happens to be written.

One more detail worth knowing: FOR JSON always wraps its output in array brackets by default, even for a single row. Add WITHOUT_ARRAY_WRAPPER, and you get back a plain JSON object instead -- useful whenever you already know the result is exactly one row.
So: AUTO infers structure from the query shape, PATH gives you explicit control through aliases, and WITHOUT_ARRAY_WRAPPER drops the brackets when you only need one object.
Next up, the reverse direction: OPENJSON, which takes a JSON string and parses it back into a rowset you can query normally.
